chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all together from Ibn Mahbub, from Abdullah ibn Sinan and Ibn Bukayr, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
He was asked about the believer who deliberately kills a believer — is there repentance for him?
So he said: If he killed him because of his faith, then there is no repentance for him.

But if he killed him out of anger, or due to some worldly matter, then his repentance is that he be subject to retaliation (qisas) from him. And if it was not known about him, he should go to the guardians of the slain and confess to them his murder of their companion.

If they then forgive him and do not execute him, he shall pay them the blood money (diya), emancipate a slave, fast two consecutive months, and feed sixty poor people — as a repentance to God, Mighty and Majestic.

key_terms.أولياء المقتول: Awliya' al-maqtul — the guardians/heirs of the slain, who hold the right of qisas or forgiveness
key_terms.الدية: Diya — blood money; financial compensation paid to the family of the deceased
key_terms.قصاص: Qisas — retaliation in kind; the legal principle of equivalent punishment for intentional killing
key_terms.نسمة: Nasama — a soul/person (in this context: a slave to be emancipated as expiation)

ai.seo_question: According to Imam al-Sadiq, what is the repentance for a believer who deliberately kills another believer?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) was asked about the conditions for repentance when a believer deliberately kills another believer. His answer distinguishes two scenarios: if the killing was religiously motivated (to suppress the victim's faith), there is absolutely no path of repentance; if it was driven by anger or worldly causes, repentance is possible through a specific process involving legal accountability, financial compensation (diya), emancipating a slave, fasting two consecutive months, and feeding sixty poor people. This hadith reflects classical Shia jurisprudence on intentional homicide (qatl al-'amd) and the intersection of legal penalties (hudud, qisas) with the spiritual possibility of divine forgiveness, addressing the community of early Muslims who would have grappled with intra-communal violence.
